step: Start with clean, conditioned hair

plain_language_guidance: Have braids installed by a professional stylist, and say something immediately if installation hurts - pain during installation means the style is too tight and the stylist should stop and loosen it.

step: Watch for early signs of traction alopecia
plain_language_guidance: If you regularly wear tight styles, check monthly for early warning signs such as broken hairs around the forehead or a receding hairline. Continued pulling can eventually stop hair growth, and the damage (traction alopecia) can become permanent the longer it goes untreated.

step: Protect hair overnight
plain_language_guidance: Pull hair back loosely under a head covering overnight; silk or satin coverings are gentler on hair than other fabrics.

plain_language_guidance: Keep braids in no longer than about 6 to 8 weeks. For weaves or extensions, limit wear to about two to three months, then take a break in a style without added hair before reinstalling.

plain_language_guidance: Wash curly or coily hair on a cycle of about once a week up to about every three weeks, rather than daily - where in that range depends on your scalp and hair. Washing too often can leave curls dry and frizzy; washing too rarely can let product buildup accumulate. Wash long or thick hair in sections.

plain_language_guidance: Condition all of your hair, not just the ends. Look for conditioners containing argan oil, glycerin, or a fatty alcohol like cetyl or stearyl alcohol. If hair is very dry or hard to detangle, conditioning before shampooing can help.

step: Safe braid removal procedure
plain_language_guidance: Trim any badly matted ends first. Unravel braids one at a time starting from the bottom, clipping away the sections you aren't working on so they don't re-tangle. Finger-detangle each section before using a wide-tooth comb, working from ends toward roots. Afterward, wash and condition thoroughly - buildup accumulates on the scalp during wear regardless of how long the style was in.
